162 - Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The: Final Fantasy is Square Enix's long-running series of Japanese role-playing games, famous since 1987 for sprawling stories of crystal mythology, doomed love, and world-ending villains like FFVI's Kefka and FFVII's Sephiroth. Its sprawling casts and playable worlds turn out to be rich philosophical material: essays here ask whether FFVII is a text players co-author, whether Kefka's nihilism refutes the heroes, whether games count as art, and how Kant, Mill, and Aristotle judge the series' many self-sacrifices, alongside the Gaia hypothesis behind the film The Spirits Within.
163 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy - L: Game of Thrones, HBO's 2011-2019 adaptation of George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire novels, is the fantasy epic famous for killing its heroes and for treating power as a blood sport among morally gray nobles. That grayness is exactly why it invites philosophy: essays here test Westeros against Hobbes on who should rule, Machiavelli on why Ned Stark and Robb fall, just war theory on Robb's campaign, and subtle puzzles about lying, misleading, and oaths, all in service of the claim that logic cuts deeper than swords.
164 - The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo an: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo is Stieg Larsson's 2005 Swedish crime novel, the first of the Millennium trilogy about journalist Mikael Blomkvist and Lisbeth Salander, the tattooed hacker with a psychiatric file who became a worldwide literary phenomenon. The books' real subject is violence against women, and the essays follow suit: Salander as a Socratic gadfly, Goffman and Foucault on how institutions label her mad, queer theory on her refusal of every identity label, Kant on sexual objectification, and even what the characters' coffee habit says about modern life.
165 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Ev: The Good Place is the NBC comedy (2016-2020) in which Eleanor Shellstrop wakes in a heaven she was mistakenly sent to and must secretly earn her place, with an actual ethics professor, Chidi, teaching her Kant and trolley problems along the way. Unusually for television, it takes moral philosophy seriously as plot, and this volume returns the favor: essays read the afterlife's points system through Hannah Arendt's bureaucracy, ask whether souls can improve after death, probe free will and bad faith, and ask who gets to decide what counts as good.
166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No: Green Lantern is the DC Comics hero whose power ring turns willpower into anything he can imagine, worn by test pilot Hal Jordan and a whole intergalactic Corps policed by the emotionless Guardians of the Universe. The premise is a philosophical engine: essays ask what role emotion should play in moral judgment when rival corps channel rage, fear, love, and hope; whether willpower is a muscle in any scientifically respectable sense; how the Guardians' reason-versus-emotion split maps onto gender; and what moral pluralism, recruitment, and Hegelian tragedy look like among lanterns.
167 - The Ultimate Harry Potter and Phil: Harry Potter is J. K. Rowling's seven-novel series (1997-2007) about a boy wizard at Hogwarts, the best-selling story of its era and a fixture of a generation's reading life. Beneath the spells lie old metaphysical puzzles, and the essays dig them out: whether souls exist and how Voldemort's Horcruxes split one, what Nearly Headless Nick's ghost implies about mind and body, whether prophecies and time turners leave any room for free will, and how the series weighs destiny against the choices that Dumbledore says define us.
168 - Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Bo: Heroes was NBC's 2006-2010 drama about ordinary people worldwide discovering extraordinary abilities, from an indestructible cheerleader to a time-traveling office worker, with the slogan 'Save the cheerleader, save the world.' Superpowers turn out to be a stress test for philosophy: essays ask whether social contract theory survives people who cannot be jailed or executed, whether great power brings great responsibility, whether the shadowy Company is justified, when insiders should blow the whistle, and whether Nietzsche's eternal recurrence or free will governs Hiro's attempts to rewrite destiny.
169 - The Hobbit and Philosophy - For Wh: The Hobbit is Tolkien's 1937 tale of Bilbo Baggins, the comfort-loving hobbit swept into a dragon hunt with thirteen dwarves, the prelude to The Lord of the Rings. The editors read it as Plato's cave allegory retold 'there and back again,' and the essays run with the journey: Aristotle and Seneca on how Bilbo's trials build virtue, Taoism on greed and letting go, walking as a philosophical practice, cosmopolitanism learned through shared adventure, and the classical ideal of glory weighed against Socrates' quieter life of the soul.
170 - House and Philosophy - Everybody L: House, the Fox medical drama (2004-2012), stars Hugh Laurie as Dr. Gregory House, a misanthropic diagnostic genius whose motto 'everybody lies' drives each week's medical mystery. The show is a sustained argument in disguise: essays here weigh House's ruthless utilitarianism against Kantian duties to patients, ask whether his candor is honesty or cruelty, probe addiction, rationality, and self-deception, and press the question the series keeps raising, whether being right about a diagnosis can ever justify trampling the person it saves.
171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Un: House of Cards is Netflix's political drama (2013-2018) following Frank Underwood, a congressman who murders, manipulates, and breaks the fourth wall on his way to the presidency, declaring 'democracy is so overrated.' The show is practically a syllabus in political philosophy: essays map Frank onto Plato's Ring of Gyges and Thrasymachus's claim that justice is the advantage of the stronger, contrast Rawls's ideal theory with Washington as it is, and read the Underwoods through Nietzsche's will to power and Scheler's ressentiment, asking what happens when the knaves write the rules.
